note: What an errand COSTS, per world, in watt-hours (pluggybot issue #15).
DATA, not code, on exactly the terms hub/rewards.json and
hub/cadence.json are: this is a measurement about a world, it wants
re-deriving whenever the world or the errand changes, and a deploy has
to be able to re-point it on a mounted volume without a rebuild --
$PLUGGY_ENERGY=/path/to/energy.json.
MEASURED, NEVER GUESSED. scripts/energy_spike.py is where every number
below comes from: it flies each errand once on an oversized pack and
reports SWAP_PICK to the end of SWAP_RETURN, which is the span the
mission loop cannot interrupt. Guessing here has already cost this repo
a fixture -- 0.35 Wh guessed for a drawing that measures 0.93, and a
recorded mission in which the robot claimed the job at 88 % and died
mid-stroke with the pen still on the fork.
`artwork` AND `answer` ARE THE DRAWING ERRAND, priced as `draw` rather
than flown separately: same tool, same board, same standoff, and the only
difference is the figure. Copying `draw` is the conservative direction --
a two-digit answer is strictly less ink than a house, and the errand has
measured ~0.74 Wh where `draw` reads 0.929.
WHERE TWO HONEST MEASUREMENTS DISAGREE, THE TABLE CARRIES THE DEARER.
An errand's cost depends on where the robot happens to be standing when
it starts: home's drawing measured 0.849 Wh from beside the rack and
0.929 Wh from the spawn pose in protocol/telemetry.home_lifecycle.
The gate's failure directions are not symmetric -- an over-estimate is a
charge the robot did not strictly need, an under-estimate is a robot
dead in the garden holding the LCD -- so the high reading wins.
errandWh       action -> Wh for the whole fetch-use-stow job. A key may
also be `action:target` (`draw:whiteboard_b`), which wins
over the bare action -- home's far whiteboard is 7 m away
through a doorway and measures 1.113 Wh against the near
one's 0.929, and one number for both either kills the
robot on the way back from the far one or prices the near
one off a demo cell entirely
defaultWh      what an action with no row costs. Omitted means 'the
dearest measured one here', which is the conservative
reading and the right one for an unpriced errand
exploreWhPerS  exploring is not an errand (it is bounded and
interruptible) but the rate is measured so a slice can
be priced in the overseer's prompt
chargeW        NET watts into the pack: 55 W of charger less the held
press. lifecycle.CHARGE_TIMEOUT is sized against this
READ THE NUMBERS AGAINST THE PACK. On the DEMO cells (room_hub 0.70 Wh,
home 1.10 Wh) one errand costs roughly one full charge, so there is no
return-trip margin to keep and hub/energy.py charges none -- every
existing mission behaves exactly as it did, and home's census (1.14 Wh
against a 0.99 Wh charged cell) is still attempted, because that is what
the committed recording shows the robot doing. On a HOSTING-sized pack
(PLUGGY_BATTERY_WH, 5-15 Wh) the same table makes the robot charge while
it still has a return trip in hand. The table does not change; what a
pack can afford does.
chargeW IS THE SLOWEST PRESS, NOT THE BEST ONE, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE.
Measured net rate into the pack over a sustained press: 19.4 W in one
approach, 39.6 W in another, 35-37 W over the whole cycles in the two
committed recordings. The spread is GEOMETRY -- how squarely the bumper
meets the pins decides how hard the wheels stall against them, and the
draw was a flat 28.6 W through the slow one. The only consumer is
lifecycle.charge_timeout, whose job is to catch a robot pressing on pins
that conduct nothing; sizing that cap off a good approach makes it fire
on a slow charge that is working, which is the one thing it must not do.

home.measuredOn: 40 Wh pack, 149 s explore, plus a 4 sim-hour unattended --pack hosting run; where the two disagree the dearer wins (whiteboard_b read 1.065 and 1.113 Wh, the census 1.104-1.245)

room_hub.measuredOn: 40 Wh pack, 29 s explore; carry cross-checked against protocol/telemetry.hub_lifecycle.jsonl.gz
